documentation:
## Multi_constraints

### What it does
This graph demonstrates several constraint systems.  These are:  hinges, sliders, springs and cone-twist constraints.  Each section is a separate browser graph and can be switched on and off (including rendering) at will.
 
### Inputs and outputs
These graphs are self-contained, every object is generated within Bifrost.  The output is to the viewport and as a rendered image.

### How it works
Each graph contains a basic example, demonstrating the named constraint:

***hinge_constraint*** is a simple pendulum, with a *hinge* constraint at the pivot of the pendulum and *generic* constraint at the end of the shaft to hold the bob on.

***slider_constraint*** is sometimes called a "piston" constraint - this is demonstrated with a simplified crank-shaft model that converts angular motion into linear motion.  The top object is the "piston" and is constrained to the lower, static object.  In-between the two objects is a rotating collider.

***spring_constraint*** is three simple springs, constrained and limited in both linear and angular motion with a stiffness and damping value set per axis.  

***cone_twist_constraint*** is a chain of constraints, each with it's own cone angle set per axis.  Changing these angles will change the behavior of the "chain".

Feel free to dive into any and all of these examples.

_notes.text: The ***rigid body id*** corresponds to the order of this array.  This is used later to control constraining one rigid body to another.

Rather than baking the instances to a mesh, this compound extracts both the render and collision geos from the instance object.

This is done for speed and is only a viable option when the instance count is low.  This graph has 8

A drag influence is used to simulate friction in the hinge.

This collider is driving the upper block (psiton collider) through the slider constraint.
the *rigid_body_id* attribute corresponds to the order of the input array of ***merge_ridgid_bodies***
This is a **slider** constraint.  It constrains the rigid bodies along a single axis, typically x.  This constraint is rotated 90 degrees as visible in the *transform* attribute

Rather than baking the instances to a mesh, this compound extracts both the render and collision geos from the instance object.

This is done for speed and is only a viable option when the instance count is low.  This graph has 3
 unique instances.

The constraints are generated here.  Each one constrains a platform to the "base" static object using a ***spring*** constraint.

The ***spring*** constraint has options for *damping* and *stiffness* for each linear axis (movement), as well as each angular axis (rotation).

Each linear and angular axis also has limits built into the constraint.  Feel free to change these values and see what happens.

The ***base_position*** being fed into the constraints are setting the axis upon which the platforms rotate.

These compounds create the three platforms that are to be constrained.  Inside each compound is a cube and a rigid body setup.  The *base_position* output is used later on to generate the pillars the platforms are sitting on.

Rather than baking the instances to a mesh, this compound extracts both the render and collision geos from the instance object.

This is done for speed and is only a viable option when the instance count is low.  This graph has 5
 unique instances.

# ConeTwist Constraint

This constraint allows rotation around a pivot point within a cone and provides twist control around the other axis.

_backdrops.title: Chain constraints - Double-click for more info

_notes.text:
Each capsule constraint is generated here and fed out.  Each object is constrained to the object before it in the chain.  Each constraint's pivot is locked to the pivot point of the previous object.

The rigid body ids and transforms increment as we go down the chain.

Rather than baking the instances to a mesh, this compound extracts both the render and collision geos from the instance object.

This is done for speed and is only a viable option when the instance count is low.  This graph has 8
 unique instances.
